Since Deja/Google is back up, but the thread hasn't been revisited, I
thought I'd post (one of?) the reasons that Monocle was banned. Maybe
this should be archived on Jeff's site or something. Anyway, this is
a pretty good one...perhaps LSJ can explain what the house rules on
Monocle were. Enjoy.

Xian

-------------------------------------------------------------

From: Alan Kwan (kw...@cs.cornell.edu)
Subject: The Indecent Proposition
Newsgroups: rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad
Date: 1995/04/26

The Indecent Proposition

A lesson in Superior Logic

by Alan Kwan

---------------------------

Conjecture: Asking a question on (P=Q) while controlling the
result of P allows one to enforce Q.

Situation: High-stacks tournament, final round. LSJ House Rules
on Monocle are in effect.

Turn 2, Logician gets out Normal and Dollface. Equip with Monocle
on Dollface successful on turn 3.

Turn 4, Logician's Untap. Question to prey:

"Taking the Indecent Proposition to be the proposition that,
from now on, you will not declare any blocking attempt nor play
any Reaction Card during ALL of my actions, AND you will not perform
any non-mandatory action for the remainder of the game; will the truth
value of the Indecent Proposition be equal to the truth value of
the proposition that the next action I declare an attempt will
be attempted by Dollface?"

Ruling Team Decision: Somehow, poor prey ends up being unable
to block nor play Reaction Cards during Logician's actions,
nor can the poor prey perform any actions (except forced hunting)
for the remainder of the game.

Turn 5, Logician's predator suffers the same fate ...

Logician easily ousts everybody around the table, as all players
just sit there, their hands put face-down on the table, sitting
ducks unable to block, play reaction cards or perform any actions ...

---------------------------

Conclusion: if the Meth. whose minion controls the Monocle has
Superior Logic, all his actions become unblockable and no one
else may perform any actions (after a few turns).

--
"Live Life with Heart."

Alan Kwan kw...@cs.cornell.edu

declare them). But then he/she just rephrases the question for next turn.

Alternatively, if you're in a real nit-picky mood you can try using alternative
definitions for some of the key words (such as "declare" or "perform). Thus you
maintain the letter (though not the intent) of the original question.
Or...since the question is so convoluted itself, you could very well simply ask
him to repeat the question. And keep insisting you don't understand what he's
asking, or the full ramifications of what he's asking...

In addition, why are we sticking to only two conditions? Why not throw a few
more "AND" statements while we're at it? ;)

Furthermore, won't this mess up the languages problems even more? Even if The
Monocle's questioning ability couldn't be abused so horribly, couldn't it still
be banned on similar grounds to Madness of the Bard?

Realistically, you only need to generate a consistent +3 intercept to
shut down stealth decks. And as long as you also have some transients
floating around to move yourself up to +4/+5 in emergencies, you
should definitely be OK.

Protean will consistently take +1 stealth actions with +2 from Earth
Control and +1 extra from Form of Mist. It's still worth your time to
block those, make them spend the cards, and "fail" to catch the Form
of Mist despite having a transient in hand; so what if they get a
Laptop at 4 stealth? They won't ever get the bleed through. Save
your panic transients for something that REQUIRES a panic, such as
that same person with the Laptop bleeding for 4 with Force of Will.
(and then you'll be glad that you've burned all their Earth Control
out of their hand early on.)

Obfuscate has the single most powerful 'sneak' card in the game,
Forgotten Labyrinth. Fortunately, it's only usable on non-bleeding
actions, which means your worst-case scenario is a Nossie vote deck
chucking these around. Superior gives +4 stealth on votes, and most
vote decks won't bother including more than a few Cloaks as backup,
with good reason. Again, your best option is to keep attempting
blocks, and burn transients as you can; a deck with inherent stealth
on its actions will include far less transient stealth than it could,
and you can often run them out of Forgotten Labyrinths, leaving them
in a real bind.

OBF bleed decks will cycle some combination of Lost in Crowds, Cloak,
and Faceless Night at you. That never comes out to more than +4, and
they have to really work at it to get that high. Again, save your
transients for when you need it, and watch out for carelessly chasing
Faceless Night with your untapped guys.

As tempting as it may be to block inferior Night Moves, do not waste
your time unless you have the cards to kill in hand. You will do
better by letting them move through their deck, and then catching them
only on the non-NM bleed actions. Elder Impersonation and Call of the
Grateful Dead -do- suck to have to defend against, but you -can- be
ready after you see the first one hit the table; it's just a lot
trickier.

Obtenebration has Shadow Play and Shroud of Night as its "stock"
stealth, but even in a vote deck, these will rarely generate much more
than a total of +3 stealth on any action. Again, save your transients
and catch what you need to.

(disclaimer: the above assumes that you are playing an intercept
deck. The construction of an intercept deck that can generate +3
intercept consistently AND kill things, while still being able to oust
its prey, is left for the reader. It's not impossible... but it's not
easy, either, which is why I point out elsewhere that stealth is still
more powerful than intercept.)

>At 1 pool, it's a bargain, when compared to London Evening Star or Sport
>Bike.

Quite. The card above (even unique) would be just painfully brutal,
especially with a Tzimisce deck.

-- Derek

Flaw: a "pure" spread isn't 16.6% in each bin.
It's 20% chance of winning (a five-player table).

Consider a "pure" game like "high card" :-)
Take 5 cards: an ace and four non-aces.
Deal them out to the players randomly. Ace gets a VP.
Repeat 5 times (5 VPs).

Percentages now look something like:

0: 32.8%
1: 41.0%
2: 20.5%
3: 5.12%
4: 0.64%
5: 0.032%

This table implies at first glance that the winner will
typically be the one with 2VP (a 2-1-1-1-0) split).
I won't bother checking to see if that's actually the
case, however.

To more adequately model V:TES, eliminate a player
after each round and, when a player gets an ace,
increase her chance of getting it again in the
future. This too is left for the interested student.

believe it's going to be a problem at all. Especially when the
alternative is outright failure - the Big Zero. I mean, look at the
math more closely.

Tourney Round: 1 2 3 Final Outcome
=========================================================
Event 1 Sweep Flop Sweep Sweep = win!
Event 2 Sweep Flop Sweep Flop = loss :(
Event 3 Sweep Flop Flop -- = loss :(
Event 4 Sweep Flop Flop -- = loss :(

In two events, the deck fails to reach the final and goes nowhere. In
one event, it reaches the final and becomes a free VP for someone. And
in one event, it wins. Where's the problem? And more importantly,
where's the desire to play the deck when you have a 75% chance of
failing miserably? I don't gamble on those odds; I'd rather have a deck
that interacts with the table more, and relies on my own skilled play,
dealmaking, and taking advantage of opportunities.

Perhaps I'm just coming at this from an odd perspective. Pool
tournaments are generally dominated by a very small group of players who
are just THAT much better than everyone else (in the UK: Hendry, White).
In one of the weekly tournaments I play in, I have the following record
over the past 8 weeks:

5 outright wins
2 second place finishes
1 third place finish (too sloshed to stand straight)

A 62.5% success ratio is ridiculously abusive, no matter what face you
want to put on it. I call it my "beer money tournament". Why do people
still play? Because they want to try to beat me, to test their skills
against one of the best. (And it's a cheap entry fee, too, and they
really don't give a damn about the money.) If the organizers wanted to
even things out a bit, they should bar me from that tournament on the
spot, or force me to give up some sort of handicap. But as it stands,
I'm totally abusing the tournament... I'm the equivalent of a broken
deck.

In contrast, if I won the tournament only 25% of the time, it CERTAINLY
wouldn't be abusive at all, and nobody would even consider forcing me to
be handicapped or barring me.

>Of course, no deck is that good. No VTES deck can guarantee a better
>than 20% success ratio against a field of identical decks.

No V:TES deck can "guarantee" ANY success ratio, IMO. Some decks will
tend to do better than others, but the nature of the game precludes any
guarantees... making a lot of that math up there worthless in practice.
